title: A die placed every dot. Who left the holes?
desc:
Every one of these 50,000 dots was placed by a die, and not one of them landed in a hole. This is the chaos game, and the fractal it draws is the Sierpinski triangle. Three corners, one dot, and a recipe that never changes: jump exactly halfway towards a corner, let a die pick which corner, mark the spot, repeat.

Three corners → a die picks one
Jump exactly half the way → mark the dot, repeat 50,000 times
The die is the only random part → the rule itself never changes
Change the fraction and you change the picture → half is a choice, not a law
Colour = the last corner chosen → which is why there are exactly three copies

WHERE THIS SITS IN MATHEMATICS
The chaos game is the random-iteration way of drawing the attractor of an iterated function system. The system is a fixed list of rules; here it is three contractions by one half, one towards each corner, and its attractor is the Sierpinski triangle — also called the Sierpinski gasket. The contraction ratio is part of the recipe rather than something nature fixes: three corners at one half give this triangle, while eight points at one third give the Sierpinski carpet, and the die is doing the same job in both. It is self-similar: every half-size copy is the whole thing again, which is why its fractal dimension is log3/log2 = 1.585, between a line and a sheet. The last corner chosen fixes which half-size copy the dot lands in, so three colours separate into the three copies exactly.

THIS SHAPE IS OVER A CENTURY OLD
• 1915 – Waclaw Sierpinski – described the curve in a note to the Paris Academy, "Sur une courbe dont tout point est un point de ramification"
• 1988 – Michael Barnsley – named the random-jump method "the chaos game", in his book Fractals Everywhere
• 1996 – Carles Puente, Jordi Romeu, Rafael Pous, Xavier Garcia and Ferran Benitez, in Barcelona – published the gasket as a multiband antenna in Electronics Letters
• Similar triangle-in-triangle patterns appear in 13th-century Cosmatesque inlay floors, centuries before anyone wrote the rule down

WHERE YOU MEET IT
• Radio engineering → the gasket cut into copper resonates at a run of frequencies, because it contains a half-size copy of itself, so one small antenna covers several bands
• Genetics → run the same game on a square with corners A, C, G and T, one jump per letter of a genome, and the pattern that appears is a fingerprint of the sequence (H J Jeffrey, Nucleic Acids Research, 1990)
• Computer graphics → the same random-iteration trick draws ferns, clouds and coastlines from a handful of rules instead of a stored picture

YOUR TURN (great for a classroom)
1. Mark three corners on paper. Start anywhere, roll a die — 1 or 2, 3 or 4, 5 or 6 for the three corners — mark the point halfway to it, and repeat forty times. What starts to appear?
2. Now use the four corners of a square, same halfway rule. A fractal, or does it just fill up?
3. Harder: keep the four corners, add the four side midpoints, and jump two thirds of the way instead of half. Can you predict the pattern before you draw it?

And one I would like answered: where have you seen this triangle of holes in a real object? An antenna, a speaker grille, a tiled floor — tell me what you have spotted.

Maths is beautiful: the die is thrown fifty thousand times and the holes land in exactly the same places.

Answer: four corners with the halfway rule gives no fractal at all — the dots spread out and fill the square evenly. Halving towards four corners is four maps at scale 1/2, and 4 × (1/2)² covers the whole square with nothing left over, so there are no gaps to see. Three corners work because 3 × (1/2)² leaves a quarter of the area uncovered, and that missing quarter is the holes. For question 3: eight points and a two-thirds jump is eight maps at scale 1/3, and it draws the Sierpinski carpet.
